title: Growth vs value, swing trading vs investing

inOneLine.simple: Growth investors pay up for companies they hope will grow fast; value investors look for low prices compared with profit. Swing traders hold for days or weeks; long-term investors hold for years.
inOneLine.balanced: [[growth-investing|Growth]] and [[value-investing|value]] are about what you pay for, and swing trading and long-term investing are about how long you hold. Each has its own risks: growth can disappoint, cheap can be cheap for a reason, swings need a [[stop-loss]], and long holds need the ability to sit through large falls.

explain.simple: A growth approach looks for companies whose revenue and profit may rise quickly, and often accepts a high price compared with today's profit. A value approach looks for companies whose price seems low compared with what they earn. Neither is "right": both can lose money. Separately, you need to decide how long you plan to hold. A swing trader aims to catch a price move over days or weeks, using the chart, a stop and a target. A long-term investor holds for years and focuses on the business itself.
explain.balanced: The style decides which questions matter. A growth buyer must ask what happens if growth slows, because a high [[pe-ratio|P/E]] can fall a long way. A value buyer must ask why the price is low: some businesses are shrinking. A swing trader needs a [[trading-plan]], position sizing and a stop, and pays the [[spread]] more often. A long-term investor still needs a plan: what would prove the idea wrong, and can they afford to hold through a big fall? Mixing the two, for example turning a failed swing trade into a "long-term investment" to avoid taking the loss, is a common trap.

assumptions: Fictional companies from the Fundamental Analysis Lab, Year 3
Example Quickling Apps Co (fictional): price 14.40 USD, EPS 0.18 USD
steps: If EPS grows 50% a year for two years: 0.18 × 1.5 × 1.5 = 0.405 USD. P/E at the same price = 14.40 ÷ 0.405 = about 35.6. Still high.
If growth stops instead and buyers will only pay a P/E of 20: price = 20 × 0.18 = 3.60 USD.
That is (14.40 − 3.60) ÷ 14.40 = 75% below today's price, with the same profit as today.

assumptions: A fictional share at 20.00 USD; 200 shares; costs ignored
Swing trader: stop at 19.00 USD, target 22.00 USD, plans to hold days to weeks
Long-term investor: no tight stop, plans to hold years
steps: Swing trader's risk = (20.00 − 19.00) × 200 = 200 USD. Reward at target = (22.00 − 20.00) × 200 = 400 USD. That is 2:1.
Long-term investor: if the price falls 30% to 14.00 USD, the paper loss is (20.00 − 14.00) × 200 = 1,200 USD.
The investor must be able to sit through that without being forced to sell, and must know what business change would make them sell.
Same share, same price, very different risks and plans.

explainSimpler: Growth: paying up for hoped-for growth. Value: looking for a low price, and asking why it is low. Swing: days to weeks with a stop. Long-term: years, judged on the business.
commonMistake: Turning a losing swing trade into a long-term investment so you do not have to take the loss. The original plan had a stop for a reason.

quickCheck.prompt: A share's P/E is 60 because buyers expect fast growth. What is the main risk?

options.text: Growth slows and the P/E falls
options.explanation: Right: if growth disappoints, the price can drop sharply even if profit holds.
No: high-P/E growth firms often pay little or no dividend.

options.text: There is no risk if the firm is good
options.explanation: No: a good business at a very high price can still be a poor investment.

quickCheck.prompt: Your swing trade hits its stop. What fits the plan?

options.text: Hold it as a long-term investment instead
options.explanation: No: that changes the plan to avoid taking the planned loss.

options.text: Buy more to lower your average price
options.explanation: No: that adds risk to an idea the stop said was wrong.

options.text: Exit as planned and review the trade
options.explanation: Right: the stop marks where the idea was wrong.

quickCheck.prompt: A share has a P/E of 4. What should a value-minded learner ask first?

options.text: Why is the price this low?
options.explanation: Right: some companies are cheap because their business is shrinking.

options.text: How quickly can I buy some shares?
options.explanation: No: a low P/E alone is not a reason to act.
No: the ticker says nothing about value.

doItNow.instructions: Before your next simulated trade on the "Practice ordinary share", write three lines: your style (swing or long-term), how long you plan to hold, and exactly what would make you exit. Then place the simulated trade and keep the note in your journal.

homework: After the simulated trade closes, write whether you followed the exit you planned.
